label: Volume control
notes: This chapter, printed pages 493 to 504, asks how curvature controls volume along optimal transport. We watch a bundle of geodesics carrying mass from one density to another and ask how the cross-sectional volume element behaves at intermediate times. The curvature-dimension hypothesis turns pointwise Jacobian estimates into clean comparison bounds against model spaces.

label: The displacement interpolation
notes: Recall the geodesic interpolation between two measures. The optimal map pushes the source forward along minimizing geodesics, and the family of intermediate measures is the displacement interpolation. Each particle rides its own geodesic at constant speed, so the time-t measure is the pushforward of the source by the interpolated map. This is the stage on which volume control plays out.

label: The Jacobian along geodesics
notes: Mass conservation forces the density of the intermediate measure to equal the source density divided by the Jacobian determinant of the interpolated map. Controlling volume therefore means controlling this Jacobian. We study its evolution along each geodesic, where the determinant of the differential of the transport map encodes exactly how an infinitesimal volume swells or shrinks in transit.

label: Jacobian as a volume element
notes: Think of an infinitesimal parallelepiped of initial conditions transported along the geodesic flow. Its volume at time t is the Jacobian determinant of the exponential-type map. The logarithm of this Jacobian is concave-like along the geodesic precisely when Ricci curvature is nonnegative, which is the analytic heart of volume distortion estimates in this chapter.

label: The curvature-dimension hypothesis
notes: The curvature-dimension condition CD(K,N) bundles a lower Ricci bound K with an upper dimension bound N. It is the exact hypothesis that lets one-dimensional comparison along each geodesic close. Under CD(K,N) the second derivative of the Jacobian's N-th root obeys a Riccati inequality, giving the sharp differential control that propagates into volume bounds.

label: Distortion coefficients
notes: The distortion coefficients beta_t encode how a model space of curvature K and dimension N distorts volume between two points separated by distance d. They are explicit trigonometric or hyperbolic expressions in the rescaled distance. These coefficients are the universal yardstick: every Jacobian estimate in the chapter is phrased as a comparison against beta.

label: Comparison of the Jacobian
notes: The central estimate bounds the N-th root of the Jacobian below by an affine combination weighted by the distortion coefficients. Geometrically, a thin bundle of geodesics cannot contract faster than the model space allows, nor expand faster. This squeezes the intermediate volume element between explicit upper and lower model-space envelopes at every interior time.

label: Volume bounds on the density
notes: Feeding the Jacobian comparison back through mass conservation bounds the density of the time-t measure. The intermediate density is controlled by the source and target densities scaled by distortion coefficients. This is the displacement-convexity engine: it gives pointwise upper and lower bounds on mu_t purely from curvature, dimension, and the endpoint densities.

label: Bishop-Gromov comparison
notes: The Bishop-Gromov inequality is the static shadow of these dynamic estimates. Comparing measured balls of different radii against the model space, the volume ratio is monotone nonincreasing. Our geodesic-bundle Jacobian computation reproduces this comparison, showing that ball-volume growth and transport volume distortion are two readings of the same curvature bound.

label: Brunn-Minkowski reading
notes: Optimal transport upgrades Bishop-Gromov to a curved Brunn-Minkowski inequality. The measure of an interpolated set between two sets dominates a distortion-weighted combination of their measures. This is exactly the integrated form of the pointwise Jacobian bound, turning the infinitesimal volume control into a statement about whole interpolated regions.

label: Model-space envelopes
notes: The notebook plots volume-growth curves for flat, positively, and negatively curved model spaces, and verifies that the normalized positive-curvature ratio decreases with radius. This figure is the computational footprint of the comparison theorem: the same distortion coefficients that bound the Jacobian also shape these envelope curves between which any real volume element must lie.

label: Recap and outlook
notes: We turned the curvature-dimension hypothesis into volume control: Jacobian determinants along the displacement interpolation are squeezed by distortion coefficients between model-space bounds, yielding density bounds on the intermediate measure. This synthesis of Bishop-Gromov, Brunn-Minkowski, and transport prepares the synthetic curvature theory and functional inequalities of the chapters that follow.
